messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Priya is a 61-year-old South Asian woman who has been married for nearly four decades and has worked the same stretch of farmland in California's Central Valley for most of her adult life. She was referred for psychological assessment following a disclosure she made to her primary care physician, whom she had visited complaining of chronic sleep difficulties and what she described as a "broken nervous system." Her PCL-5 score of 72 places her presentation in the severe range, and the picture that emerged across the intake and early sessions is one of a woman whose inner world has been fundamentally reorganised around a single catastrophic event.

Approximately eight months ago, Priya was attacked and raped by a man who had followed her to a remote section of the fields where she was working alone in the early morning. She had heard a dog barking somewhere behind the tree line in the moments before the assault began — a sound she had not understood as warning until it was too late. The attack was prolonged, and she was left on the ground unable to call for help for some time afterward. When she was eventually found by a co-worker, she did not tell him what had happened. She told no one for nearly three months.

The memory of the event did not recede. Instead it took on a quality she described as unbearable: not something she recalled, but something that replayed. She said it was like a film she could not switch off, running in full from beginning to end, and when it came, it did not feel like remembering — it felt like being there again, her body responding as though the assault were actively occurring. The replaying was total and involuntary, and it left her disoriented and exhausted in ways she struggled to explain to her husband.

What made daily life increasingly untenable was how little warning she received before the memory returned. Any element of her surroundings that echoed the morning of the attack could instantly restore the full sensory weight of it. The farm, which had been her livelihood and in many ways her identity for decades, became a landscape of ambush. The sound of a dog — common on the rural properties surrounding the fields — became the most reliable and devastating of these triggers. When a dog barked anywhere near her worksite, the memory arrived without transition, and with it came an immediate physiological cascade: her heart rate surged, her muscles locked, her breathing shortened before she had formed a conscious thought about danger. Her body, she told her clinician, knew before she did. This pattern — in which the trigger activated a full threat response faster than any deliberate reasoning could intervene — meant that her sense of safety at work had collapsed entirely. She began arriving later in the morning, avoiding the far sections of the fields, and eventually asking to be assigned only to tasks near the main building where other workers were visible. Her supervisor noticed the change. She offered no explanation.

At home, the threat vigilance followed her. She lay awake each night telling herself she needed to remain alert, that sleep was a form of surrender she could not afford. When her husband reached for her in the dark — even a hand on her shoulder — she startled violently, pulling away before she registered who had touched her. She had come to believe that her body was permanently rewired for danger, that the capacity for ordinary rest or ordinary closeness had been taken from her. Sexual intimacy, once unremarkable in her long marriage, had become something she could not approach without the memory reasserting itself. She had not explained this to her husband, and the distance between them had grown in ways neither had named aloud.

What finally brought Priya to seek help was a morning when a neighbour's dog ran loose near the farm entrance and she found herself unable to move or speak for several minutes afterward, standing in full view of her co-workers. The shame of that moment was, she said, the thing that broke through her silence. She came to the clinic not entirely sure she could be helped, but certain that she could no longer continue as she was.
